doc.title: Oliver Nelson Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 10, 2020

title: Teaching at IU and the music industry class
summary: As a full-time musician and adjunct at IU, he teaches jazz for listeners and a music business class, telling students schools don't prepare them for real work.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Yeah. You’ve paid some dues. If you went to a cocktail party and someone that you’d never met said, “Well Mr. Nelson, what do you do for a living?” Do you have a short answer?

Oh yeah. I am a full time musician now, and I’ve never — I’ve always wanted to do that but now I actually am because I’m teaching adjunct at IU, I’m teaching a jazz for listeners class, which is an introductory class for people that are not in jazz and know

nothing about it at all. I taught a beginning jazz improv class and we had people in there that couldn’t play a blues scale, didn’t know what a blues scale was and all that kind of stuff and that was really good. And then I picked up teaching a music industry class. And that class is interesting because what I found out, Monk, is most of the students have no clue of how the music business works. I mean they can play their instruments really well, but I said, “When you get out, how are you going to eat? You know how are you going to pay your rent? How are you going to pay your car note?” And some of them have no clue. And they would say, “Well you know Mr. Nelson, I play in the top orchestra at IU.” I say, “Well you know what? You’re paying IU to play in that orchestra. You want somebody to pay you to play. So how are you going to make that happen?” And some of them start to get it but then it really makes them kind of think a little bit because schools do really not do a good job of really letting students know what the real world of music is out here. And with Covid it makes it that much different.

I know I have trouble, I’ve had trouble over the years trying to get my students to realize that they can’t just play what they want to if they want to work. You’ve got to be prepared for any situation, be able to take requests, and so it’s tricky. I’m going to guess that you learned what the word “gig” meant early on in life.
